                       UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
6                    WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON                           
                               AT SEATTLE                                     
7                                                                             
     STEVEN FLOYD, et al.,           CASE NO. C22-1599-KKE                    
8                                                                             

                   Plaintiff(s),     ORDER GRANTING MOTION TO                 
9                                                                             
          v.                         COMPEL                                   

10                                                                             
     AMAZON.COM INC., et al.,                                                 

11                                                                             
                    Defendant(s).                                             

12                                                                             
         Months after Defendant Apple Inc. served discovery requests on Plaintiff Steven Floyd, 
13                                                                             
    who was at the time the sole named plaintiff in this putative class action, and long after the 
14                                                                             
    responses to those requests were due and remain unanswered, Floyd seeks to—in response to 
15                                                                             
    Apple’s motion to compel—withdraw as a named plaintiff, dismissing his claims without prejudice 
16                                                                             
    to remain an absent class member.  Apple does not oppose Floyd’s withdrawal, but requests that 
17                                                                             
    the Court first compel him to respond to the outstanding discovery requests and appear for a 
18                                                                             
    deposition that was noticed by Apple and Defendant Amazon.com Inc. (“Amazon”) before he 
19                                                                             
    sought to withdraw.  Because the Court finds that Defendants would suffer prejudice if Floyd were 
20                                                                             
    permitted to withdraw without responding to the outstanding requests for discovery and testifying 
21                                                                             
    at a deposition, the Court will grant Apple’s motion to compel and defer ruling on Floyd’s motion 
22                                                                             
    to withdraw until after he has complied with these discovery conditions.  
23                                                                             

24                                                                             
1                         I.   BACKGROUND                                     
2        This case was filed in November 2022 as a putative class action with Floyd as the sole 
3   named plaintiff, alleging that he was overcharged when he purchased a new Apple product on 

4   Amazon’s website as a result of the Global Tenets Agreement between Defendants.  See, e.g., Dkt. 
5   No. 1 ¶ 22.  Since the time of filing, the parties have briefed two rounds of motions to dismiss, a 
6   contested  motion  to  amend  the  complaint,  and  several  discovery  disputes  requiring  Court 
7   intervention.  Dkt. Nos. 30, 32, 42, 43, 53, 76, 80, 89, 90.              
8        Defendants served requests for production on Floyd, and his counsel objected on multiple 
9   general and specific grounds in October 2023.  See Dkt. No. 90 at 31–75.  Floyd has not produced 
10   any documents in response to those requests (or any others).  Dkt. No. 104 at 6.  On February 8, 
11   2024, Apple served interrogatories on Floyd, seeking information about his purchases and use of 
12   smartphones and tablets, as well as the purchases and uses of his household members.  Dkt. No. 

13   90 at 10.  On February 13, Floyd’s counsel responded to Apple, explaining that Floyd had “become 
14   difficult to reach” but had “not withdrawn as a class representative[.]”  Dkt. No. 105 at 6.  
15   Defendants replied on February 22, inquiring as to (among other things) Floyd’s availability for a 
16   deposition.  Id. at 5.  His counsel responded the next day that they would not be able to provide 
17   information about Floyd’s availability until they heard from Floyd himself.  Id.  On February 26, 
18   Defendants indicated that they had “no choice but to issue a notice” for Floyd’s deposition if his 
19   counsel could not provide an available date.  Id. at 4.                   
20        Floyd’s counsel moved for leave to amend the complaint on February 29, seeking to add 
21   two new named plaintiffs but not, at that time, seeking to withdraw Floyd.  Dkt. No. 80.  Apple 
22   opposed that motion on the grounds that Floyd was an improper class representative from the 

23   inception of this case, and that it was unfair that Defendants had been forced to respond to 
24   discovery while this case proceeded with one inadequate named plaintiff.  Dkt. No. 86.  Apple 
1   noted that it had “devoted significant time and expense to discovery, and served requests for 
2   production  and  interrogatories  that  have  been  frustrated  by  Floyd’s  failure  to  respond 
3   substantively.”  Id. at 14.  Defendants argued in the alternative that if new plaintiffs are added, 

4   Floyd’s  counsel  should  be  required  to  show  that  the  Court  should  stay  discovery  against 
5   Defendants to allow them to minimally test whether the new representatives would be adequate 
6   class representatives before requiring Defendants to expend resources on discovery.  Id. at 17–18. 
7        On March 11, 2024, Floyd’s counsel provided “objections and response” to Apple’s 
8   interrogatories (Dkt. No. 90 at 21–28), lodging what Apple characterizes as “boilerplate and 
9   conclusory objections” with no actual information from Floyd, and no indication that the document 
10   was prepared with Floyd’s input or participation.  Dkt. No. 104 at 6.     
11        The Court granted Floyd’s motion for leave to amend on May 6, and Floyd and the new 
12   named Plaintiffs filed a second amended complaint the next day, on May 7.  See Dkt. Nos. 98, 99.  

13   On May 8, Amazon served a notice of Floyd’s deposition on Plaintiffs’ counsel for May 28.  Dkt. 
14   No. 105 at 9.  In that notice, Amazon explained that it “expects that Mr. Floyd will answer 
15   interrogatories and produce responsive documents to Amazon’s outstanding discovery requests … 
16   at least 10 days before the deposition.”  Id.  Plaintiffs’ counsel responded on May 10 that they 
17   would produce Floyd for a deposition if he reengaged with them.  Id. at 20.  Floyd did not reengage, 
18   appear for the deposition, or respond to any of the outstanding discovery requests.   
19        Apple filed this motion to compel Floyd to respond to the discovery requests and appear 
20                                                                             
    for a deposition.  Dkt. No. 104.1  In response/opposition, Plaintiffs’ counsel cross-moved to 
21   withdraw Floyd as a named plaintiff, although Floyd intends to remain an absent class member.  
22   Dkt. No. 114.  In a consolidated reply/response, Apple agrees that Floyd may withdraw as a named 
23                                                                             

24   1 Amazon concurred in the motion as well.  See Dkt. No. 104 at 5 n.1.     
1   plaintiff if he chooses, but insists that his withdrawal should be conditioned on his testifying for a 
2   deposition and responding to the discovery requests that were propounded or noticed while he 
3   remained a named Plaintiff (as he does to this day).  Dkt. No. 125.  Defendants contend that they 

4   would be prejudiced if the Court allows Floyd to avoid his discovery obligations as a party simply 
5   by withdrawing.  Id. at 10.                                               
6        Apple’s motion to compel and Floyd’s motion to withdraw are now ripe for resolution, and 
7                                                                             
    the Court has considered the parties’ briefing2 and heard oral argument on both motions.  For the 
8   following reasons, the Court will grant Apple’s motion to compel and defer ruling on Floyd’s 
9   motion to withdraw.                                                       
10                              II.  ANALYSIS                                  
11        The burden to obtain discovery of any kind from absent class members is very high. See, 
12   e.g., Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts, 472 U.S. 797, 810 n.2 (1985) (noting that burdens, including 
13   discovery, “are rarely imposed upon plaintiff class members”).  On the other hand, by filing a 
14   lawsuit in a putative class action, a named plaintiff is obligated to “participate in discovery and 
15   provide testimony.”  Fraley v. Facebook Inc., No. C 11-1726-LHK (PSG), 2012 WL 555071, at 
16   *3  (N.D.  Cal.  Feb.  21,  2012).    The  scope  of  discovery  is  broad,  restricted  only  to  “any 
17   nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional to the needs 
18   of the case[.]”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1).                                
19        Apple contends that the discovery it seeks to compel from Floyd is relevant to: (1) class-
20   certification issues (whether the new named Plaintiffs are typical and adequate representatives of 
21   class members like Floyd); (2) the merits determination of the relevant market; (3) whether Floyd 
22   is a “core customer” referenced in the operative complaint (Dkt. No. 99 ¶ 91) based on his 

23                                                                             

    2 This order refers to the parties’ briefing using CM/ECF page numbers.   
24                                                                             
1   purchasing behavior; (4) whether Plaintiffs are correct that Apple’s device records are inaccurate 
2   (as they have alleged); and (5) Defendants’ defenses pertaining to the statute of limitations and 
3   whether  the  putative  class  members  suffered  an  antitrust  injury.    Dkt.  No.  125  at  12–14.  

4   Accordingly, Apple requests that Floyd be compelled to respond to the outstanding discovery and 
5   testify at a deposition before he is permitted to withdraw as a named plaintiff.  Dkt. No. 104. 
6        Plaintiffs contend that the discovery Apple seeks to compel has limited relevance, and go 
7   on to argue that even if the discovery was relevant, it is not necessary or proportional to the needs 
8   of the case because there are other named Plaintiffs who are ready and willing to respond to 
9   discovery.  Dkt. No. 127 at 4.  Given that Floyd does not want to continue as a named Plaintiff, 
10   and Defendants do not seek to force him to do so, Plaintiffs argue that discovery responses from 
11   the named Plaintiffs other than Floyd are sufficient for Defendants’ purposes.  Id. at 8. 
12        Discovery conditions are sometimes, but not always, imposed on a withdrawing named 

13   plaintiff.  Compare, e.g., Benanav v. Healthy Paws Pet Ins. LLC, No. 2:20-cv-0421-LK, 2023 WL 
14   5227702, at *9–10 (W.D. Wash. Aug. 15, 2023) (where a named plaintiff sought to dismiss his 
15   claims with prejudice, court conditioned dismissal on his providing discovery responses and sitting 
16   for a two-hour deposition limited to issues unique to him); Gallegos v. Atria Management Co., No. 
17   ED  CV  16-888-JGB  (SPx),  2016  WL  11824850,  at  *5  (C.D.  Cal.  Nov.  14,  2016) 
18   (“[N]otwithstanding  [named  plaintiff’s]  uncertain  status,  the  information  defendants  request 
19   remains relevant.  Although it would not necessarily be proper for defendants to seek such 
20   documents from other putative class members at this point, because [named plaintiff] initiated this 
21   action and was the only named plaintiff until a month ago, it is appropriate for defendants to seek 
22   such documents from her.”); Fraley, 2012 WL 555071, at *3 (requiring an outgoing named 

23   plaintiff to appear for a deposition); with, e.g., In re MGM Resorts Int’l Data Breach Litig., No. 
24   2:20-cv-000376-GMN-NJK, 2024 WL 1440902, at *4 (D. Nev. Apr. 2, 2024) (finding that because 
1   dismissing named plaintiffs without conditions “would not deprive [Defendant] of discovery on 
2   uniquely  situated  class  members”  no  unfair  prejudice  would  result  from  the  unconditional 
3   withdrawal of the named plaintiffs); Doe v. Ariz. Hosp. & Healthcare Ass’n, No. CV 07-1292-

4   PHX-SRB, 2009 WL 1423378, at *14 (D. Ariz. Mar. 19, 2009) (declining to impose dismissal 
5   conditions, finding them “particularly unnecessary in light of the fact that there are currently three 
6   identified class representatives who could be … deposed in her stead”).   
7        The Court finds that based on the circumstances of this case, granting Apple’s motion to 
8   compel before turning to consider Floyd’s motion to withdraw is appropriate.  Defendants’ 
9   discovery requests were served long before Floyd sought to withdraw, and most of them were 
10   propounded when Floyd was the sole named Plaintiff.  The Court is satisfied that the discovery 
11   Apple seeks is relevant to its defenses as well as to some of the issues related to class certification 
12   even if Floyd will not be a named plaintiff at that stage.  See Dkt. No. 131 at 42–48 (Apple’s 

13   arguments regarding the relevance of the Floyd discovery requests with respect to the definition 
14   of the relevant market, whether households with Amazon Prime memberships are “locked in” to 
15   purchasing products from Amazon as alleged in the complaint (see, e.g., Dkt. No. 99 ¶¶ 36, 101, 
16   119), whether an antitrust injury occurred, whether the named Plaintiffs’ claims are typical of the 
17   putative class (that would include Floyd)).                               
18        Apple has further explained how the “limited information” that Defendants have been able 
19   to obtain about Floyd to date confirms that he possesses information relevant to the merits of this 
20   litigation as well as class certification.  See Dkt. No. 131 at 49.  Although Plaintiffs dispute (see, 
21   e.g., id. at 56–59) whether the discovery sought by Defendants will be, ultimately, persuasive as 
22   to any claim or defense of this case, or as to class-certification inquiries, they have not shown that 

23   the information sought does not meet the low threshold of relevance or that it is not proportional 
24                                                                             
1   to the needs of the case.  Under these circumstances, Defendants are entitled to the discovery they 
2   seek from Floyd, before he is permitted to withdraw as a named Plaintiff. 
3        Plaintiffs suggest that discovery conditions are inappropriate based on the posture of this 

4   case, arguing that Defendants would not be prejudiced by Floyd’s withdrawal this early in the 
5   litigation (Dkt. No. 127 at 9, Dkt. No. 131 at 55).  Their characterization of the stage of the 
6   proceedings as “early” is somewhat disingenuous, however, given that the proceedings have been 
7   protracted significantly due to Floyd’s non-responsiveness.  That Floyd sought to withdraw 
8   “before a single responsive document was produced” (Dkt. No. 127 at 9) does not alone establish 
9   that Defendants would not be prejudiced by his withdrawal, given that “Floyd’s allegations alone 
10   formed the basis of the initial and First Amended Complaint, and it is against his sole allegations 
11   that Defendants have had to defend for nearly two years.”  Dkt. No. 125 at 15.   
12        Because Apple has shown that the information it seeks from Floyd is sufficiently relevant, 

13   because Floyd has a unique status as the original sole named plaintiff and he possesses information 
14   that may not be identical to information available from the other named plaintiffs, and because 
15   Apple propounded much of this discovery long before Floyd sought to withdraw, the Court finds 
16   that it is appropriate to compel him to respond and testify at a deposition before allowing Floyd to 
17   withdraw.  See Dysthe v. Basic Rsch., L.L.C., 273 F.R.D. 625, 628–29 (C.D. Cal. 2011) (finding 
18   that because a defendant is entitled to depose a named plaintiff, and the named plaintiff has 
19   information that is relevant to the litigation even if he eventually withdraws, the defendant was 
20   entitled to depose named plaintiff before withdrawal); see also Gallegos,  2016 WL 11824850, at 
21   *5 (compelling a named plaintiff who had filed a motion to withdraw to nonetheless respond to 
22   discovery requests seeking relevant information, noting that “[a]lthough it would not necessarily 

23   be proper for defendants to seek such documents from other putative class members at this point, 
24                                                                             
1   because [plaintiff] initiated this action and was the only named plaintiff until a month ago, it is 
2   appropriate for defendants to seek such documents from her”).             
3                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  

4        For these reasons, the Court GRANTS Apple’s motion to compel (Dkt. No. 104), and 
5   DEFERS ruling on Plaintiffs’ cross-motion to withdraw (Dkt. No. 114).  Floyd is ORDERED to 
6   respond to the outstanding interrogatories and requests for production addressed in Apple’s motion 
7   no later than August 30, 2024.  No later than September 30, 2024, Floyd shall testify at a deposition 
8   to be scheduled at a mutually agreeable time.                             
9        If Floyd complies with these conditions, the parties may file a stipulated motion permitting 
10   Floyd to withdraw as a named plaintiff.  The clerk is directed to TERMINATE Plaintiffs’ cross-
11   motion to withdraw (Dkt. No. 114), subject to renewal if necessary.       
12        Dated this 16th day of August, 2024.                                 

13                                                                             
                                  A                                           
14                                                                             
                                  Kymberly K. Evanson                         
15                                 United States District Judge                

16                                                                             

17                                                                             
18                                                                             
19                                                                             
20                                                                             
21                                                                             
22                                                                             
23

6   proceedings as “early” is somewhat disingenuous, however, given that the proceedings have been 
7   protracted significantly due to Floyd’s non-responsiveness.  That Floyd sought to withdraw 
8   “before a single responsive document was produced” (Dkt. No. 127 at 9) does not alone establish 
9   that Defendants would not be prejudiced by his withdrawal, given that “Floyd’s allegations alone 
10   formed the basis of the initial and First Amended Complaint, and it is against his sole allegations 
11   that Defendants have had to defend for nearly two years.”  Dkt. No. 125 at 15.   
12        Because Apple has shown that the information it seeks from Floyd is sufficiently relevant, 

13   because Floyd has a unique status as the original sole named plaintiff and he possesses information 
14   that may not be identical to information available from the other named plaintiffs, and because 
15   Apple propounded much of this discovery long before Floyd sought to withdraw, the Court finds 
16   that it is appropriate to compel him to respond and testify at a deposition before allowing Floyd to 
17   withdraw.  See Dysthe v. Basic Rsch., L.L.C.,
273 F.R.D. 625
, 628–29 (C.D. Cal. 2011) (finding 
18   that because a defendant is entitled to depose a named plaintiff, and the named plaintiff has 
19   information that is relevant to the litigation even if he eventually withdraws, the defendant was 
20   entitled to depose named plaintiff before withdrawal); see also Gallegos,
2016 WL 11824850
, at 
21   *5 (compelling a named plaintiff who had filed a motion to withdraw to nonetheless respond to 
22   discovery requests seeking relevant information, noting that “[a]lthough it would not necessarily 

23   be proper for defendants to seek such documents from other putative class members at this point, 
24                                                                             
1   because [plaintiff] initiated this action and was the only named plaintiff until a month ago, it is 
2   appropriate for defendants to seek such documents from her”).             
3                           III.  CONCLUSION                                  

4        For these reasons, the Court GRANTS Apple’s motion to compel (Dkt. No. 104), and 
5   DEFERS ruling on Plaintiffs’ cross-motion to withdraw (Dkt. No. 114).  Floyd is ORDERED to 
6   respond to the outstanding interrogatories and requests for production addressed in Apple’s motion 
7   no later than August 30, 2024.  No later than September 30, 2024, Floyd shall testify at a deposition 
8   to be scheduled at a mutually agreeable time.                             
9        If Floyd complies with these conditions, the parties may file a stipulated motion permitting 
10   Floyd to withdraw as a named plaintiff.  The clerk is directed to TERMINATE Plaintiffs’ cross-
11   motion to withdraw (Dkt. No. 114), subject to renewal if necessary.
